The abbreviations and terms of art this proposal uses, each defined once in plain words. Where a term names a document, the definition says who issues it.

<!-- keep -->
| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **ADP** | Annual Development Plan. The county's one-year plan, drawn from the CIDP, that names the projects and programmes for the coming financial year. Prepared by the county executive. |
| **CFSP** | County Fiscal Strategy Paper. The county treasury's annual paper that sets the resource envelope and the ceilings for each sector in the next budget. Tabled before the county assembly. |
| **CIDP** | County Integrated Development Plan. The county's five-year development plan, required by the County Governments Act 2012, against which the ADP and the budget are meant to be set. |
| **ECVR** | Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration. The IEBC's registration drives held in phases ahead of the 2027 general election, on top of the continuous registration it runs at its offices. |
| **Equitable share** | The part of nationally raised revenue that is shared among the 47 counties by the formula the Commission on Revenue Allocation recommends and Parliament approves. It is the largest single item in a county's resource envelope. |
| **GOTV** | Get out the vote. The final phase of a campaign, in which effort moves from persuading voters to making sure supporters actually turn out on polling day. |
| **IEBC Forms 34 to 39** | The statutory results forms, one series per elective office: 34 for president, 35 for member of the National Assembly, 36 for member of the county assembly, 37 for governor, 38 for senator and 39 for woman representative. The A form records the count at a polling station; the B and C forms record the tallies at constituency and county level. |
| **NG-CDF** | National Government Constituencies Development Fund. The national fund, set up under the NG-CDF Act 2015, that finances projects such as classrooms and bursaries in each constituency, overseen by the area's member of Parliament. |
| **Own-source revenue** | The revenue a county raises itself, from fees, charges, licences and local levies, as distinct from transfers from the national government. |
| **USSD** | Unstructured Supplementary Service Data. The short-code menus (dialled as *code#) that work on any mobile phone, including basic phones without data, and on every network. |

first12: The campaign runs a lean core: a small steering team that owns
note: Chapter merge (consolidation Step 4): team moved into engagement, word for word, under "The team".
text:
The campaign runs a lean core: a small steering team that owns campaign strategy, narrative discipline and data integrity, and **subcontracts specialised work** (video production, audio jingles, media buying, USSD gateway infrastructure and event staging) to specialist vendors. Firefly joins that structure as its intelligence layer — it is not one of the execution packages, and it does not replace the publishing team.

```figure
id: org-chart
```

**Three cores, and they are not the same team.**

*   **The campaign's command structure** — the Campaign Manager and three functional leads in the
    chart above. Four roles. Firefly works to it and replaces no part of it.
*   **Dr. Mulu's existing digital team** — the people producing and publishing the daily record
    today, led by the campaign's **Digital Director**. This engagement adds a brief to their week. It does not add a manager to their line.
*   **The Firefly core** — strategy, analysis and the offline layer: three people at Standard and Premium, two at Lean with the offline-layer operator part-activated (Section 21.1).

```figure
id: fig-5-9-team
```

Where this chapter says "four-person core" it means the campaign's; where Section 21.1 says "3-person core" it means Firefly's; "your team" means the one already in post. The **Digital Director** named in the runbooks (Annex F) and in Section 15.4.4 is the head of that team, a campaign role. Other campaign-side roles named in this proposal (for example the owners of the objectives in Section 8.2) are the campaign's to appoint.

*Corrected: earlier versions said the three-person Firefly core is named at every engagement level; at Lean it is two people and a part-activated operator, as Section 21.1 states.*

What the arrangement buys, stated without the usual claims about bloat:

1.  **Decisions in one place.** A single named campaign-side counterpart approves, and a single
    Firefly director briefs. Campaigns fail digitally when five people can commission content and
    no one can approve it.
2.  **Operational security by compartment.** External vendors work under NDAs that expose the
    specific creative brief, not the overarching strategy.
3.  **Capacity that scales without a standing department.** Surge roles activate against a named
    phase or KPI trigger and stand down again, so nothing is retained through a quiet fortnight
    simply because it was hired.
4.  **Specialist quality where it is measurable.** Vernacular recording and telecom infrastructure
    are bought from people who do only that.

**A lean core with a defined surge.** Firefly delivers this engagement through a small senior core team supplemented
by named surge roles activated at specific phases and engagement levels. This is
stated plainly because a campaign is entitled to know exactly who is doing the
work. A proposal claiming a large standing department it does not have will
fail on the first question about it.

The structure below scales with the service level selected in Section 21.1.

**The service-delivery tracker is Firefly's to build and operate; the owned platforms stay with your team.** **Split ownership, and the split matters.** The tracker is new infrastructure nobody currently runs. The owned platforms stay with your team, who run them now and will continue to; Firefly's contribution there is the brief, the calendar and the approval gate.

*The single clearest expression of the candidate's actual
professional discipline.*

#### Why it exists

Every candidate in this race will promise water points, roads and markets. Only
one is professionally qualified in **verifying whether promises were kept**. A
public service-delivery tracker is not a campaign gadget; it is that
qualification, running in public, before the election rather than after it.

#### What it is

A simple public tool through which any Kitui resident can report and follow up
on a local service-delivery issue — a broken water point, an impassable feeder
road, a market without sanitation, a stalled project.

**Deliberately multi-channel, because the people with the most to report have
the least connectivity:**

```visual
kind: checklist
items:
  - label: "USSD"
    text: "The campaign shortcode → option 3 → **works on any phone, no internet**"
  - label: "SMS"
    text: "Text the issue to the campaign shortcode"
  - label: "WhatsApp"
    text: "Message the campaign line"
  - label: "Web"
    text: "Simple mobile-first form, WCAG compliant"
  - label: "Ward champion"
    text: "Report in person; champion logs it"
```

#### What happens to a report

```figure
id: fig-5-2-1-report-flow
```

#### Design principles

```visual
kind: checklist
items:
  - label: "Public by default"
    body: "The register is visible to anyone, mapped by ward, with counts by category. Transparency is the point."
  - label: "No personal data published"
    body: "Reports appear with ward, category and status only. Contact details are used to update the reporter and nothing else, under the Section 19.3 charter."
  - label: "Outcomes published honestly — including failures"
    body: "Where an issue is not resolved, the register says so. A tracker that only shows successes is marketing, and voters recognise it instantly. Publishing unresolved items is what makes the resolved ones credible."
  - label: "No false authority"
    body: "Dr. Mulu is not the county government. The tracker records what was reported, what was raised, and what happened — never implying powers he does not hold. Overclaiming here would invite exactly the attack the tool exists to pre-empt."
  - label: "Continues after the election"
    body: "Stated up front. A tracker that closes on polling day was a campaign tactic; one that continues is a governance commitment — and the commitment is the persuasive element."
```

#### What it is worth to the campaign

```visual
kind: checklist
items:
  - label: "Narrative"
    body: "the strongest possible proof of the Verification pillar (Section 10.1) — evidence rather than assertion"
  - label: "Data"
    body: "the issues citizens report, ward by ward, counted from what arrives rather than assumed, feeding directly into the weekly brief"
  - label: "Organising"
    body: "every report is a consented contact and a warm lead for ward champions"
  - label: "Earned media"
    body: "a public register of county service-delivery failures is a standing story for county correspondents (Section 15.2.2)"
  - label: "Defensive"
    body: "it makes \"he is not close to ordinary people\" a difficult attack to sustain against a candidate publishing their reported problems"
```

#### Build

Built on the USSD and SMS layer Firefly operates (Section 15.3.3), plus a lightweight public register on the campaign site. **It reuses a
layer the campaign is building anyway; nothing comparable exists in this race.**

#### The opening register: the county's own scorecard

The tracker does not start from an empty list. The county's *Delivering the Kitui Promise* scorecard (August 2022 – August 2025) claims {{scorecard.claimed}} projects and itemises {{scorecard.itemised}} of them with value, ward and status, KSh {{scorecard.itemised.ksh|bn}} billion in all (Tier 1 as a record of what the county claims, not evidence that the claims are true). Those rows load as the tracker's opening register ([kitui-scorecard-projects.csv](/data/kitui-scorecard-projects.csv)): each becomes a public row, *County says: complete. Residents say: ___*, and reports through USSD option 3 fill the second column.

The first verification questions are inconsistencies inside the county's document or against an official statistic. Each is a question to publish and test, not an accusation, and a county correspondent can check the first six independently (Section 15.2.2).

```visual

title: "The tracker's first questions"
items:
  - label: "Q1. Livestock vaccinated"
    text: "{{scorecard.vaccinated}} claimed (Tier 1, county scorecard); the itemised rows total {{scorecard.vaccinated.itemised}} animals (calculated)."
  - label: "Q2. Infant mortality"
    text: "Claimed to fall from {{scorecard.imr.from}} to {{scorecard.imr.to}} per thousand births; KDHS 2022 puts Kitui at {{health.imr}}. Is the scorecard's figure a facility rate or a county rate?"
  - label: "Q3. Roads graded"
    text: "{{scorecard.roads.graded}} km claimed; the itemised row of {{scorecard.roads.row.km}} km (Tier 1) comes to KSh {{scorecard.roads.row.per-km}} a km (calculated)."
  - label: "Q4. Boreholes"
    text: "{{scorecard.boreholes.drilled}} drilled and {{scorecard.boreholes.equipped}} equipped: are the rest not yet equipped?"
  - label: "Q5. Health beneficiaries"
    text: "Two health projects list {{scorecard.health.beneficiaries}} beneficiaries (Tier 1, county scorecard), more than the county's 2019 population of {{census.population}}: a catchment, not people served?"
  - label: "Q6. The unitemised projects"
    text: "{{scorecard.claimed}} claimed, {{scorecard.itemised}} itemised: where is the list of the other {{scorecard.unitemised}} (calculated)?"
  - label: "Q7. Kangu Kangu"
    text: "KSh {{scorecard.kangu.ksh|m1}} million for {{scorecard.kangu.households}}+ households (Tier 1, county scorecard), commissioned after the period the scorecard covers: what has been delivered since?"
  - label: "Q8. Boda boda sheds"
    text: "{{scorecard.boda.sheds}} claimed; {{scorecard.boda.sheds.itemised}} itemised."
  - label: "Q9. Ward attributions"
    text: "Some rows place wards in the wrong constituency (Voo/Kyamatu under Kitui South; it is in Kitui East): a data-quality point for any ward-level use."
```

| Reports received | {{target.tracker.phase-1}} | {{target.tracker.phase-2}} | {{target.tracker.phase-3}} |

#### The service-delivery performance tracker

The campaign builds and maintains the **Kitui County Service-Delivery Performance Tracker**, a live analytical dashboard and open-data ledger that serves a dual purpose: during the campaign, it operates as an **irrefutable evidence asset** countering opposition claims. Its scope is the citizen-report register above, with Dr. Mulu's verified NG-CDF record as its proof layer. Turning it into a **Governor's Day-One Public Delivery Dashboard** after the election is a pledge Dr. Mulu may choose to make, not a deliverable of this engagement: until he holds office it must never imply powers he does not hold.

```figure
id: delivery-tracker
```

#### Dual Operational Function:

1.  **As a Campaign Credibility Asset (Pre-Election):**
    *   *Public Web & USSD Transparency:* Voters can dial `*[shortcode]#` or visit the web portal to query exact project GPS coordinates, contract values, and completion certificates in their own village.
    *   *Debate & Media Weapon:* Equips candidate and spokespersons with instant, primary-sourced factual data to rebut rival exaggerations on live radio and television debates.
2.  **As a Day-One Governing Tool (Post-Election; a pledge Dr. Mulu may make, not a deliverable of this engagement):**
    *   *Statutory Ward Equalization Tracking:* Establishes the operational framework for managing ward development funds allocated by the published, needs-weighted formula that replaced the Ksh {{policy.ward-fund|m}} million equal-ward guarantee (Section 10.1), tracking execution velocity and contractor payments across all 40 wards in real time.
    *   *Zero Pending Bills Enforcer:* Integrates directly into the County Treasury accounting system to ensure all ward projects are verified before invoice settlement, preventing the recurrence of county debt.

#### Candidate media training

Three sessions, plus refreshers:

1. **Core message discipline** — bridging from any question to the Economist
Governor narrative without appearing evasive; keeping economic explanation
under 30 seconds without losing accuracy. The characteristic risk for a
technically expert candidate is answering at the length the question
deserves rather than the length the audience will hold.
2. **Hostile interview and radio phone-in** — handling interruption, aggressive
framing, and callers on stations with rival-aligned ownership; the discipline
of never repeating a hostile framing in the answer.
3. **Debate performance** — the 60-second answer, the memorable close, the
prepared pivot, and handling direct attack without appearing rattled.

**Refreshers** before each debate or major forum, plus a recorded mock with
playback review.

#### The debate and forum playbook

**Preparation:**

* Full briefing pack: rival positions, likely lines of attack, verified
counter-data with sources
* Mock debate with a stand-in playing the leading rival
* Three prepared "moments" — a memorable, quotable formulation for each of the
top three issues

**Live clipping operation:**

|---|---|---|
| Live | Editor monitors and marks clip points in real time | Video editor |
| +5 min | First clip cut, subtitled in Kiswahili | Video editor |
| +15 min | Published across Facebook, X, TikTok, Instagram | Community managers |
| +30 min | Kikamba-subtitled version published | Content lead |
| +45 min | WhatsApp-optimised version to ward champions | Volunteer coordinator |
| +60 min | Audio-only version for radio and voice-note distribution | Content lead |
| +2 hours | SMS with a link, or a plain-text key line, to consented contacts in relevant wards | Paid media manager |
| Next day | Long-form cut to YouTube; written summary to Tier A journalists | Content lead |

**The rule: the clip is published before the coverage is written.** Whoever
distributes the moment first defines what the debate was about.

To win fair coverage on national and regional outlets without paying for access to broadcast gatekeepers, the press desk pitches evidence first:

1.  **Hansard and audit exclusives:** verified, data-rich policy briefs for national bureau chiefs (*Daily Nation, Standard, Citizen TV, KTN News*) on national debt, equalisation-fund legislation and the county's pending bills.
2.  **Project tours:** accredited regional correspondents taken to Kitui Central projects (solar boreholes, TVET workshops, secondary-school laboratories), with on-camera interviews with the people they serve.
3.  **The right of reply:** using the statutory right of reply under the Media Council of Kenya (MCK) Act whenever a rival station misrepresents the candidate's record.

**Lines for likely attacks.** The pre-drafted response lines for the debate and the phone-in are kept with the holding positions, in Annex F.3.

**Owner: Firefly, end to end.** Two pieces of infrastructure, held and run by Firefly: the **WhatsApp Business API line** and the **USSD shortcode**. It is also the one place where Firefly is a **data controller or joint controller** rather than a processor — see Section 19.1, which must be settled in writing before the first dispatch.

#### Why this layer decides the race

**{{ict.internet}}%** of Kitui's residents use the internet and **{{ict.phone}}%** own a mobile phone (CA/KNBS
2023/24, Tier 1). Nationally, smartphones are {{ict.smartphone-share}}% of active SIMs (CA Q3 FY2025/26, Tier 2),
meaning feature phones remain a substantial share, and disproportionately so in rural, older and
lower-income populations.

Put plainly: **a purely digital campaign in Kitui addresses roughly one in
four residents, and the three it misses are concentrated in exactly the wards
where Dr. Mulu's recognition deficit is largest.**

The phone side of this layer is larger than the resident rate suggests. Adults own phones at {{ict.phone.adult}}% (KDHS 2022), so about {{reach.phone.adult}} voters can receive an SMS or dial a USSD menu, against about {{reach.phone.resident}} on the resident rate (both modelled, Section 4.3). On its own logic that makes this the layer that decides the race: it reaches roughly three voters in four.

This is not an equity footnote. It is the central strategic problem of
campaigning in this county, and solving it is the clearest demonstration of the
"Economist Governor" proposition: allocating resources to where the need is,
rather than where measurement is convenient.

The critical constraint: the campaign can only message consented numbers
(Section 19.1). List building is therefore a KPI in its own right from Phase −1,
not an afterthought — consented contacts are a campaign asset that compounds.

#### The SMS layer

**Consent-first architecture.** Every number in the campaign database arrives
by opt-in: a USSD self-registration, a signed baraza sheet with a clear data
notice, a WhatsApp opt-in confirmation, a website form, or a missed-call
opt-in. **No purchased lists. Ever.** See Section 19.2 for the
regulatory basis; the short version is that the industry code requires express
opt-in for political messages and the ODPC has demonstrated willingness to
penalise unsolicited messaging.

> ### Bulk political SMS cannot be sent in Kikamba
>
> The CA/NCIC guidelines on political bulk messaging restrict political SMS to **English or
> Kiswahili** (Tier 1, Communications Authority). They also require every bulk political message
> to be **lodged with the mobile operator at least 48 hours before sending**, with the verbatim
> text and a signed authorisation, and they allow the operator to **refuse** a non-compliant
> message outright.
>
> **This changes the channel plan, not the language strategy.** Kikamba remains the campaign's
> strongest register — it simply cannot ride the bulk SMS rail. It belongs on **radio, WhatsApp
> voice notes, USSD menu text, barazas and person-to-person**, which is where the Section 12.6
> pillars already put it. SMS carries the Kiswahili and English versions of the same message.
>
> Two practical consequences the operating rhythm must absorb: a 48-hour lodging lead time makes
> **same-day SMS rapid response impossible** — the rebuttal row below runs on WhatsApp and radio
> instead — and a **2020 draft revision** proposed narrowing the sending window to 08:00–18:00
> `[VERIFY whether in force]`.

**Message architecture** — 160 characters, **English or Kiswahili only**, ward-tagged:

| Type | Frequency | Language | Example structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Policy drop** | Weekly | Kiswahili / English | One issue, one commitment, one verification promise |
| **Community message** | Fortnightly | Kiswahili | Policy anchor in plain register. *The Kikamba proverb version of this message goes out as a WhatsApp voice note, not as SMS* |
| **Registration drive** | Phase-specific | Kiswahili / English | Deadline, nearest centre, what to bring |
| **Event notice** | As scheduled | Kiswahili | Ward-targeted baraza details |
| **GOTV sequence** | Final 30 days | Kiswahili / English | Countdown, polling station, time |
| **Rapid rebuttal** | On trigger | — | **Not an SMS channel.** The 48-hour lodging rule rules it out; runs on WhatsApp, radio and the ward networks |

```visual

title: "Operational discipline"
items:
  - label: "Every bulk send lodged with the operator 48 hours ahead"
    body: ", verbatim text plus signed authorisation, logged against the dispatch record"
  - label: "No attacks on individuals, families, ethnicity, religion or association"
    body: "in any message — a guideline requirement, and already a charter commitment (Section 19.3, clauses 2 and 6)"
  - label: "Sending window **7am–7pm**, per market practice and DND norms"
  - label: "Every message carries a clear opt-out; opt-outs honoured immediately and permanently"
  - label: "Ward-tagged segmentation so a message about mango prices reaches Kitui West and not Kyuso"
  - label: "Personalisation by first name where consent covers it"
  - label: "Per-send audit trail retained, per the charter (Section 19.3)"
```

#### The USSD layer

USSD works on every phone, requires no internet, and is close to free for the
voter. It is the single most under-used civic channel in Kenyan county
politics.

**Proposed menu — dialled on the campaign's USSD shortcode:**

```figure
id: fig-5-2-3-ussd-menu
```

**Why option 3 matters most.** The service-delivery tracker (Section 15.1.1) is
reachable from a feature phone in Mutha. A constituent reports a broken water
point by dialling a short code; the report enters a public register; the
campaign follows up and publishes the outcome. That is the M&E credential
operating in public, before the election, on the cheapest possible technology.

**Set-up:** 5–7 working days for a shared code; 2–4 weeks for a dedicated code
pending operator approval.

#### Voice and audio

* **Kikamba voice notes from Dr. Mulu** distributed by WhatsApp and by ward
champions to Bluetooth-share onward. Audio travels where text does not, and
carries the candidate's actual voice — the highest-trust format available.
* **Radio** — see Section 15.2.2.
* **Audio versions of all flagship policy content**, addressing both low
literacy ({{edu.none.women}}% of women and {{edu.none.men}}% of men aged six and over have no education) and low bandwidth.

#### The mobile-money agent network

Kenya's registered mobile-money agents grew from **{{ict.agents.2025}} in September 2025 to
{{ict.agents}} in March 2026** — expanding roughly four times faster than
subscriptions. In rural Kitui, the agent kiosk is often the most reliable
commercial touchpoint in a settlement.

```visual
kind: cards
preset: agent
items:
  - title: "The mobile-money agent network: proposed use"
    text: "agent-sited printed materials carrying QR codes and the USSD"
    fields:
      - { label: "Conditions", text: "- **This is a distribution channel, not a data channel.** The campaign does not seek, receive or process any customer data from agents. Nothing about transaction records, balances or customer identity enters this programme.\n- Participation is by the proprietor's consent and is disclosed as campaign material.\n- `[Confirm approach with campaign counsel — agent networks are regulated financial infrastructure and any commercial arrangement should be reviewed]`" }
```

#### KPIs for the offline layer

| Metric | Phase −1 | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Phase 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Consented SMS contacts | {{target.sms.phase-1}} | {{target.sms.phase-1b}} | {{target.sms.phase-2}} | **{{target.sms}}** |
| USSD unique sessions | Not live | {{target.ussd.phase-1}} | {{target.ussd.phase-2}} | {{target.ussd.phase-3}} |
| Issue reports via tracker | Not live | {{target.tracker.phase-1}} | {{target.tracker.phase-2}} | {{target.tracker.phase-3}} |
| Opt-out rate | <2% | <2% | <2% | <2% |
| Wards with active SMS presence | 15 | 40 | 40 | 40 |

**Opt-out rate is the health metric.** A rising opt-out rate means the campaign
is being experienced as spam, which damages the brand of rigour and
accountability the whole strategy rests on. It is treated as a red-flag KPI, not
a vanity one.

A precise campaign needs a data layer it can trust. No loose spreadsheets, unverified voter claims or ad-hoc phone lists: one structured database, with provenance and audit trails on every record, run within Kenyan privacy law.

This section defines the voter and supporter data model and the legal compliance workflows under Kenya's **Data Protection Act (DPA) 2019** and the **Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC)**. The three-tier provenance standard that grades every figure in this proposal (Annex A.1.1) and the protocol for when two sources disagree (Annex A.1.3) are set out alongside the evidence they govern.


#### The voter and supporter data model

The campaign database is organized around a relational, entity-attribute-value schema optimized for speed, geographic aggregation, and privacy segmentation. Every supporter record is linked to an exact geographic locus and carries timestamped consent metadata:

```figure
id: supporter-schema
```

```visual
kind: checklist
title: "Key Architecture Principles"
items:
  - label: "Strict Anonymization & Encryption at Rest"
    body: "PII (Personally Identifiable Information), including mobile MSISDNs, is encrypted using **AES-256-GCM**. Read-only analytic dashboards (such as ward target monitors) access only hashed identifiers (`msisdn_hash`) and geographic aggregates."
  - label: "Granular Geographic Tagging"
    body: "No supporter entry exists in a vacuum; every record MUST map to an explicit Constituency, Ward, and Polling Station."
  - label: "Audit Trail Logging"
    body: "Every modification to a voter's `support_status` or contact detail logs the modifying user ID, timestamp, and field collection source."
```

*The Data Protection Act obligations this layer works under, and its mandatory compliance safeguards, are set out with the rest of compliance in 19.2.*

```visual
  - when: "Phase 1–2"
    label: "2 — Predictive"
    text: "Voter scoring live; field-digital loop operating; audience segments driven by score"
    fields:
      - { label: "Prerequisite", text: "**Section 19.2 compliance gate cleared**" }
      - { label: "Owner", text: "Data Analyst (surge)" }
  - when: "Phase 2–3"
    label: "3 — Attributed"
    text: "Multi-touch attribution; offline conversion tracking; effort per persuaded voter reported against actuals"
    fields:
      - { label: "Prerequisite", text: "Stage 2 stable ≥ 6 weeks" }
      - { label: "Owner", text: "Data Analyst" }
  - when: "Phase 3"
    label: "4 — Optimised"
    text: "Continuous reallocation against modelled marginal return; GOTV list prioritisation"
    fields:
      - { label: "Prerequisite", text: "Stage 3 validated against field returns" }
      - { label: "Owner", text: "Data Analyst + Director" }
```

**No stage is skipped.** A campaign that attempts predictive scoring before its
tagging is consistent produces confident nonsense, and a campaign that attempts
it before the compliance gate produces legal exposure.

#### Who owns the data

A **single named data-governance owner** is accountable for both analytics
performance and data compliance — deliberately one role, because splitting them
creates an incentive to treat compliance as someone else's obstacle.

Responsibilities:

* Maintains the data inventory: what is held, lawful basis, retention period,
who has access
* Owns the consent audit trail and can produce it on demand within
**24 hours** — the standard the Annex F.6 drill tests
* Owns the deletion schedule and executes it (Section 19.3)
* Is the campaign's standing point of contact for the Section 19.2 compliance
reviewer
* Holds authority to **suspend any targeting activity** pending review, without
requiring commercial sign-off

At Lean this role sits with the Digital Director, who heads the campaign's existing digital team; from Standard it sits with the Data Analyst / Modeller (Section 17.2). It is named in writing either way.
